If you want to obtain the minimum value in one step, you can use the following:

Returns a mutable pointer to the underlying integer.

Doing non-atomic reads and writes on the resulting integer can be a data race.
This method is mostly useful for FFI, where the function signature may use
`*mut usize` instead of `&AtomicUsize`.

Returning an `*mut` pointer from a shared reference to this atomic is safe because the
atomic types work with interior mutability. All modifications of an atomic change the value
through a shared reference, and can do so safely as long as they use atomic operations. Any
use of the returned raw pointer requires an `unsafe` block and still has to uphold the same
restriction: operations on it must be atomic.

# Default in core::default - Rust

Source: https://edp.fortanix.com/docs/api/core/default/trait.Default.html

## Expand description

A trait for giving a type a useful default value.

Sometimes, you want to fall back to some kind of default value, and
don’t particularly care what it is. This comes up often with `struct`s
that define a set of options:

How can we define some default values? You can use `Default`:

```
#[derive(Default)]
struct SomeOptions {
    foo: i32,
    bar: f32,
}
fn main() {
    let options: SomeOptions = Default::default();
}
```
[Run](https://play.rust-lang.org/?code=%23!%5Ballow(unused)%5D%0A%23%5Ballow(dead_code)%5D%0A%23%5Bderive(Default)%5D%0Astruct%20SomeOptions%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20foo%3A%20i32%2C%0A%20%20%20%20bar%3A%20f32%2C%0A%7D%0A%0Afn%20main()%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20let%20options%3A%20SomeOptions%20%3D%20Default%3A%3Adefault()%3B%0A%7D&edition=2018)

Now, you get all of the default values. Rust implements `Default` for various primitives types.

If you want to override a particular option, but still retain the other defaults:

This trait can be used with `#[derive]` if all of the type’s fields implement
`Default`. When `derive`d, it will use the default value for each field’s type.

Provide an implementation for the `default()` method that returns the value of
your type that should be the default:

Returns the “default value” for a type.

Default values are often some kind of initial value, identity value, or anything else that may make sense as a default.

Using built-in default values:

```
let i: i8 = Default::default();
let (x, y): (Option<String>, f64) = Default::default();
let (a, b, (c, d)): (i32, u32, (bool, bool)) = Default::default();
```

# AtomicU64 in core::sync::atomic - Rust

Source: https://edp.fortanix.com/docs/api/core/sync/atomic/struct.AtomicU64.html

`#[repr(C, align(8))]pub struct AtomicU64 { /* fields omitted */ }`## Expand description

An integer type which can be safely shared between threads.

This type has the same in-memory representation as the underlying
integer type, [ u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html). For more about the differences between atomic types and
non-atomic types as well as information about the portability of
this type, please see the

[module-level documentation](https://edp.fortanix.com/index.html).

**Note:** This type is only available on platforms that support
atomic loads and stores of [ u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html).

Get atomic access to a `&mut u64`.

**Note:** This function is only available on targets where `u64` has an alignment of 8 bytes.

```
#![feature(atomic_from_mut)]
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
let mut some_int = 123;
let a = AtomicU64::from_mut(&mut some_int);
a.store(100, Ordering::Relaxed);
assert_eq!(some_int, 100);
```

`Relaxed`[makes the load part](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Release)

## 👎 Deprecated since 1.50.0: Use `compare_exchange` or `compare_exchange_weak` instead

Use `compare_exchange` or `compare_exchange_weak` instead

Stores a value into the atomic integer if the current value is the same as
the `current` value.

The return value is always the previous value. If it is equal to `current`, then the
value was updated.

`compare_and_swap` also takes an [ Ordering](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html) argument which describes the memory
ordering of this operation. Notice that even when using

[, the operation might fail and hence just perform an](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.AcqRel)

`AcqRel``Acquire` load, but not have `Release` semantics.
Using [makes the store part of this operation](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Acquire)

`Acquire`[if it happens, and using](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`[makes the load part](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Release)

`Release`[.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`**Note**: This method is only available on platforms that support atomic operations on
[ u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html).

`compare_and_swap` is equivalent to `compare_exchange` with the following mapping for
memory orderings:

| Original | Success | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| Relaxed | Relaxed | Relaxed |
| Acquire | Acquire | Acquire |
| Release | Release | Relaxed |
| AcqRel | AcqRel | Acquire |
| SeqCst | SeqCst | SeqCst |

`compare_exchange_weak` is allowed to fail spuriously even when the comparison succeeds,
which allows the compiler to generate better assembly code when the compare and swap
is used in a loop.

```
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
let some_var = AtomicU64::new(5);
assert_eq!(some_var.compare_and_swap(5, 10, Ordering::Relaxed), 5);
assert_eq!(some_var.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 10);
assert_eq!(some_var.compare_and_swap(6, 12, Ordering::Relaxed), 10);
assert_eq!(some_var.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 10);
```
[Run](https://play.rust-lang.org/?code=%23!%5Ballow(unused)%5D%0Afn%20main()%20%7B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Async%3A%3Aatomic%3A%3A%7BAtomicU64%2C%20Ordering%7D%3B%0A%0Alet%20some_var%20%3D%20AtomicU64%3A%3Anew(5)%3B%0A%0Aassert_eq!(some_var.compare_and_swap(5%2C%2010%2C%20Ordering%3A%3ARelaxed)%2C%205)%3B%0Aassert_eq!(some_var.load(Ordering%3A%3ARelaxed)%2C%2010)%3B%0A%0Aassert_eq!(some_var.compare_and_swap(6%2C%2012%2C%20Ordering%3A%3ARelaxed)%2C%2010)%3B%0Aassert_eq!(some_var.load(Ordering%3A%3ARelaxed)%2C%2010)%3B%0A%7D&edition=2018)

Stores a value into the atomic integer if the current value is the same as
the `current` value.

The return value is a result indicating whether the new value was written and
containing the previous value. On success this value is guaranteed to be equal to
`current`.

`compare_exchange` takes two [ Ordering](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html) arguments to describe the memory
ordering of this operation.

`success` describes the required ordering for the
read-modify-write operation that takes place if the comparison with `current` succeeds.
`failure` describes the required ordering for the load operation that takes place when
the comparison fails. Using [as success ordering makes the store part of this operation](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Acquire)

`Acquire`[, and using](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`[makes the successful load](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Release)

`Release`[. The failure ordering can only be](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`[,](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.SeqCst)

`SeqCst`[or](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Acquire)

`Acquire`[and must be equivalent to or weaker than the success ordering.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`**Note**: This method is only available on platforms that support atomic operations on
[ u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html).

```
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
let some_var = AtomicU64::new(5);
assert_eq!(some_var.compare_exchange(5, 10,
                                     Ordering::Acquire,
                                     Ordering::Relaxed),
           Ok(5));
assert_eq!(some_var.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 10);
assert_eq!(some_var.compare_exchange(6, 12,
                                     Ordering::SeqCst,
                                     Ordering::Acquire),
           Err(10));
assert_eq!(some_var.load(Ordering::Relaxed), 10);
```

Stores a value into the atomic integer if the current value is the same as
the `current` value.

Unlike [ AtomicU64::compare_exchange](https://edp.fortanix.com/struct.AtomicU64.html#method.compare_exchange),
this function is allowed to spuriously fail even
when the comparison succeeds, which can result in more efficient code on some
platforms. The return value is a result indicating whether the new value was
written and containing the previous value.

`compare_exchange_weak` takes two [ Ordering](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html) arguments to describe the memory
ordering of this operation.

`success` describes the required ordering for the
read-modify-write operation that takes place if the comparison with `current` succeeds.
`failure` describes the required ordering for the load operation that takes place when
the comparison fails. Using [as success ordering makes the store part of this operation](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Acquire)

`Acquire`[, and using](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`[makes the successful load](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Release)

`Release`[. The failure ordering can only be](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`[,](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.SeqCst)

`SeqCst`[or](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Acquire)

`Acquire`[and must be equivalent to or weaker than the success ordering.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`**Note**: This method is only available on platforms that support atomic operations on
[ u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html).

```
use std::sync::atomic::{AtomicU64, Ordering};
let val = AtomicU64::new(4);
let mut old = val.load(Ordering::Relaxed);
loop {
    let new = old * 2;
    match val.compare_exchange_weak(old, new, Ordering::SeqCst, Ordering::Relaxed) {
        Ok(_) => break,
        Err(x) => old = x,
    }
}
```

Fetches the value, and applies a function to it that returns an optional
new value. Returns a `Result` of `Ok(previous_value)` if the function returned `Some(_)`, else
`Err(previous_value)`.

Note: This may call the function multiple times if the value has been changed from other threads in
the meantime, as long as the function returns `Some(_)`, but the function will have been applied
only once to the stored value.

`fetch_update` takes two [ Ordering](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html) arguments to describe the memory ordering of this operation.
The first describes the required ordering for when the operation finally succeeds while the second
describes the required ordering for loads. These correspond to the success and failure orderings of

[respectively.](https://edp.fortanix.com/struct.AtomicU64.html#method.compare_exchange)

`AtomicU64::compare_exchange`Using [ Acquire](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Acquire) as success ordering makes the store part

`Relaxed`[makes the final successful load](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Release)

`Release`[. The (failed) load ordering can only be](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

`Relaxed`[,](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.SeqCst)

`SeqCst`[or](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Acquire)

`Acquire`[and must be equivalent to or weaker than the success ordering.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Ordering.html#variant.Relaxed)

[ u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html).

```

let x = AtomicU64::new(7);
assert_eq!(x.fetch_update(Ordering::SeqCst, Ordering::SeqCst, |_| None), Err(7));
assert_eq!(x.fetch_update(Ordering::SeqCst, Ordering::SeqCst, |x| Some(x + 1)), Ok(7));

[Run](https://play.rust-lang.org/?code=%23!%5Ballow(unused)%5D%0Afn%20main()%20%7B%0Ause%20std%3A%3Async%3A%3Aatomic%3A%3A%7BAtomicU64%2C%20Ordering%7D%3B%0A%0Alet%20foo%20%3D%20AtomicU64%3A%3Anew(23)%3B%0Aassert_eq!(foo.fetch_min(42%2C%20Ordering%3A%3ARelaxed)%2C%2023)%3B%0Aassert_eq!(foo.load(Ordering%3A%3ARelaxed)%2C%2023)%3B%0Aassert_eq!(foo.fetch_min(22%2C%20Ordering%3A%3ARelaxed)%2C%2023)%3B%0Aassert_eq!(foo.load(Ordering%3A%3ARelaxed)%2C%2022)%3B%0A%7D&edition=2018)

If you want to obtain the minimum value in one step, you can use the following:

Returns a mutable pointer to the underlying integer.

Doing non-atomic reads and writes on the resulting integer can be a data race.
This method is mostly useful for FFI, where the function signature may use
`*mut u64` instead of `&AtomicU64`.

Returning an `*mut` pointer from a shared reference to this atomic is safe because the
atomic types work with interior mutability. All modifications of an atomic change the value
through a shared reference, and can do so safely as long as they use atomic operations. Any
use of the returned raw pointer requires an `unsafe` block and still has to uphold the same
restriction: operations on it must be atomic.

# core - Rust

Source: https://edp.fortanix.com/docs/api/core/index.html

## Expand description

**You are viewing the documentation of the Rust core library as a part of
the Fortanix Rust EDP.** There are no changes compared to the normal the
core library.

The Rust Core Library is the dependency-free 1 foundation of

[The Rust Standard Library](https://edp.fortanix.com/std/index.html). It is the portable glue between the language and its libraries, defining the intrinsic and primitive building blocks of all Rust code. It links to no upstream libraries, no system libraries, and no libc.

The core library is *minimal*: it isn’t even aware of heap allocation,
nor does it provide concurrency or I/O. These things require
platform integration, and this library is platform-agnostic.

Please note that all of these details are currently not considered stable.

This library is built on the assumption of a few existing symbols:

-
`memcpy`,`memcmp`,`memset`- These are core memory routines which are often generated by LLVM. Additionally, this library can make explicit calls to these functions. Their signatures are the same as found in C. These functions are often provided by the system libc, but can also be provided by the[compiler-builtins crate](https://crates.io/crates/compiler_builtins).
-
`rust_begin_panic`- This function takes four arguments, a`fmt::Arguments`, a`&'static str`, and two`u32`’s. These four arguments dictate the panic message, the file at which panic was invoked, and the line and column inside the file. It is up to consumers of this core library to define this panic function; it is only required to never return. This requires a`lang`attribute named`panic_impl`.
-
`rust_eh_personality`- is used by the failure mechanisms of the compiler. This is often mapped to GCC’s personality function, but crates which do not trigger a panic can be assured that this function is never called. The`lang`attribute is called`eh_personality`.

# core::option - Rust

Source: https://edp.fortanix.com/docs/api/core/option/index.html

## Expand description

Optional values.

Type [ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) represents an optional value: every

[is either](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[and contains a value, or](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some`[, and does not.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[types are very common in Rust code, as they have a number of uses:](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`- Initial values
- Return values for functions that are not defined over their entire input range (partial functions)
- Return value for otherwise reporting simple errors, where `None`
- Optional struct fields
- Struct fields that can be loaned or “taken”
- Optional function arguments
- Nullable pointers
- Swapping things out of difficult situations

[ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)s are commonly paired with pattern matching to query the presence
of a value and take action, always accounting for the

[case.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None````
fn divide(numerator: f64, denominator: f64) -> Option<f64> {
    if denominator == 0.0 {
        None
    } else {
        Some(numerator / denominator)
    }
}
// The return value of the function is an option
let result = divide(2.0, 3.0);
// Pattern match to retrieve the value
match result {
    // The division was valid
    Some(x) => println!("Result: {}", x),
    // The division was invalid
    None    => println!("Cannot divide by 0"),
}
```
[Run](https://play.rust-lang.org/?code=%23!%5Ballow(unused)%5D%0Afn%20main()%20%7B%0Afn%20divide(numerator%3A%20f64%2C%20denominator%3A%20f64)%20-%3E%20Option%3Cf64%3E%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20if%20denominator%20%3D%3D%200.0%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20None%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%20else%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Some(numerator%20%2F%20denominator)%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%7D%0A%0A%2F%2F%20The%20return%20value%20of%20the%20function%20is%20an%20option%0Alet%20result%20%3D%20divide(2.0%2C%203.0)%3B%0A%0A%2F%2F%20Pattern%20match%20to%20retrieve%20the%20value%0Amatch%20result%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%20The%20division%20was%20valid%0A%20%20%20%20Some(x)%20%3D%3E%20println!(%22Result%3A%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20x)%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%20The%20division%20was%20invalid%0A%20%20%20%20None%20%20%20%20%3D%3E%20println!(%22Cannot%20divide%20by%200%22)%2C%0A%7D%0A%7D&edition=2018)

Rust’s pointer types must always point to a valid location; there are
no “null” references. Instead, Rust has *optional* pointers, like
the optional owned box, `Option``<``Box<T>``>`.

The following example uses [ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) to create an optional box of

[. Notice that in order to use the inner](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)

`i32`[value, the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html)

`i32``check_optional` function first needs to use pattern matching to
determine whether the box has a value (i.e., it is [) or not (](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some(...)`[).](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None````
let optional = None;
check_optional(optional);
let optional = Some(Box::new(9000));
check_optional(optional);
fn check_optional(optional: Option<Box<i32>>) {
    match optional {
        Some(p) => println!("has value {}", p),
        None => println!("has no value"),
    }
}
```
[Run](https://play.rust-lang.org/?code=%23!%5Ballow(unused)%5D%0Afn%20main()%20%7B%0Alet%20optional%20%3D%20None%3B%0Acheck_optional(optional)%3B%0A%0Alet%20optional%20%3D%20Some(Box%3A%3Anew(9000))%3B%0Acheck_optional(optional)%3B%0A%0Afn%20check_optional(optional%3A%20Option%3CBox%3Ci32%3E%3E)%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20match%20optional%20%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20Some(p)%20%3D%3E%20println!(%22has%20value%20%7B%7D%22%2C%20p)%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%20%20%20%20None%20%3D%3E%20println!(%22has%20no%20value%22)%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%7D%0A%7D%0A%7D&edition=2018)

Rust guarantees to optimize the following types `T` such that
[ Option<T>](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) has the same size as

`T`:- `Box<U>`
- `&U`
- `&mut U`
- `fn`,- `extern "C" fn`
- `num::NonZero*`
- `ptr::NonNull<U>`
- `#[repr(transparent)]`struct around one of the types in this list.

This is called the “null pointer optimization” or NPO.

It is further guaranteed that, for the cases above, one can
[ mem::transmute](https://edp.fortanix.com/mem/fn.transmute.html) from all valid values of

`T` to `Option<T>` and
from `Some::<T>(_)` to `T` (but transmuting `None::<T>` to `T`
is undefined behaviour).In addition to working with pattern matching, [ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) provides a wide
variety of different methods.

The [ is_some](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.is_some) and

[methods return](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.is_none)

`is_none`[if the](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`true`[is](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[or](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some`[, respectively.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`- `as_ref`- `&Option<T>`to- `Option<&T>`
- `as_mut`- `&mut Option<T>`to- `Option<&mut T>`
- `as_deref`- `&Option<T>`to- `Option<&T::Target>`
- `as_deref_mut`- `&mut Option<T>`to- `Option<&mut T::Target>`
- `as_pin_ref`- `Pin`- `<&Option<T>>`to- `Option<`- `Pin`- `<&T>>`
- `as_pin_mut`- `Pin`- `<&mut Option<T>>`to- `Option<`- `Pin`- `<&mut T>>`

These methods extract the contained value in an [ Option<T>](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) when it
is the

[variant. If the](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some`[is](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[:](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`- `expect`
- `unwrap`
- `unwrap_or`
- `unwrap_or_default`- `T`(which must implement the- `Default`
- `unwrap_or_else`

These methods transform [ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) to

- `ok_or_else`- `Some(v)`- `Ok(v)`- `None`- `Err`

These methods transform the [ Some](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some) variant:

- `filter`- `t`if the- `Option`- `Some(t)`- `Some(t)`- `true`; otherwise, returns- `None`
- `flatten`- `Option<Option<T>>`
- `map`- `Option<T>`- `Option<U>`- `Some`- `None`

`U`:- `map_or`- `Some`- `Option`- `None`

`Option`- `zip`- `Some((s, o))`- `self`is- `Some(s)`- `Option`- `Some(o)`- `None`
- `zip_with`- `f`and returns- `Some(f(s, o))`- `self`is- `Some(s)`- `Option`- `Some(o)`- `None`

These methods treat the [ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) as a boolean value, where

[acts like](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some`[and](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`true`[acts like](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[. There are two categories of these methods: ones that take an](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`false`[as input, and ones that take a function as input (to be lazily evaluated).](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`The [ and](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.and),

[, and](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.or)

`xor`[as input, and produce an](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[as output. Only the](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[method can produce an](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.and)

`and`[value having a different inner type](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option<U>``U` than
[.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option<T>`| method | self | input | output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `and` | `None` | (ignored) | `None` |
| `and` | `Some(x)` | `None` | `None` |
| `and` | `Some(x)` | `Some(y)` | `Some(y)` |
| `or` | `None` | `None` | `None` |
| `or` | `None` | `Some(y)` | `Some(y)` |
| `or` | `Some(x)` | (ignored) | `Some(x)` |
| `xor` | `None` | `None` | `None` |
| `xor` | `None` | `Some(y)` | `Some(y)` |
| `xor` | `Some(x)` | `None` | `Some(x)` |
| `xor` | `Some(x)` | `Some(y)` | `None` |

The [ and_then](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.and_then) and

[methods take a function as input, and only evaluate the function when they need to produce a new value. Only the](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.or_else)

`or_else`[method can produce an](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.and_then)

`and_then`[value having a different inner type](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option<U>``U` than [.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option<T>`| method | self | function input | function result | output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `and_then` | `None` | (not provided) | (not evaluated) | `None` |
| `and_then` | `Some(x)` | `x` | `None` | `None` |
| `and_then` | `Some(x)` | `x` | `Some(y)` | `Some(y)` |
| `or_else` | `None` | (not provided) | `None` | `None` |
| `or_else` | `None` | (not provided) | `Some(y)` | `Some(y)` |
| `or_else` | `Some(x)` | (not provided) | (not evaluated) | `Some(x)` |

This is an example of using methods like [ and_then](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.and_then) and

[in a pipeline of method calls. Early stages of the pipeline pass failure values (](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.or)

`or`[) through unchanged, and continue processing on success values (](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[). Toward the end,](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some`[substitutes an error message if it receives](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.or)

`or`[.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None````
let mut bt = BTreeMap::new();
bt.insert(20u8, "foo");
bt.insert(42u8, "bar");
let res = vec![0u8, 1, 11, 200, 22]
    .into_iter()
    .map(|x| {
        // `checked_sub()` returns `None` on error
        x.checked_sub(1)
            // same with `checked_mul()`
            .and_then(|x| x.checked_mul(2))
            // `BTreeMap::get` returns `None` on error
            .and_then(|x| bt.get(&x))
            // Substitute an error message if we have `None` so far
            .or(Some(&"error!"))
            .copied()
            // Won't panic because we unconditionally used `Some` above
            .unwrap()
    })
    .collect::<Vec<_>>();
assert_eq!(res, ["error!", "error!", "foo", "error!", "bar"]);
```

`Option<T>`[implementation. With this order,](https://edp.fortanix.com/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)

`PartialOrd`[compares as less than any](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[, and two](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some`[compare the same way as their contained values would in](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some``T`.  If `T` also implements

`Ord`[.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option<T>`An [ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) can be iterated over. This can be helpful if you need an
iterator that is conditionally empty. The iterator will either produce
a single value (when the

[is](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[), or produce no values (when the](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some`[is](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[). For example,](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[acts like](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#method.into_iter)

`into_iter`[if the](https://edp.fortanix.com/iter/fn.once.html)

`once(v)`[is](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[, and like](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.Some)

`Some(v)`[if the](https://edp.fortanix.com/iter/fn.empty.html)

`empty()`[is](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option`[.](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`Iterators over [ Option<T>](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) come in three types:

- `into_iter`- `Option`
- `iter`- `&T`to the contained value
- `iter_mut`- `&mut T`to the contained value

An iterator over [ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) can be useful when chaining iterators, for
example, to conditionally insert items. (It’s not always necessary to
explicitly call an iterator constructor: many

[methods that accept other iterators will also accept iterable types that implement](https://edp.fortanix.com/iter/trait.Iterator.html)

`Iterator`[, which includes](https://edp.fortanix.com/iter/trait.IntoIterator.html)

`IntoIterator`[.)](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html)

`Option````
let yep = Some(42);
let nope = None;
// chain() already calls into_iter(), so we don't have to do so
let nums: Vec<i32> = (0..4).chain(yep).chain(4..8).collect();
assert_eq!(nums, [0, 1, 2, 3, 42, 4, 5, 6, 7]);
let nums: Vec<i32> = (0..4).chain(nope).chain(4..8).collect();
assert_eq!(nums, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]);

One reason to chain iterators in this way is that a function returning
`impl Iterator` must have all possible return values be of the same
concrete type. Chaining an iterated [ Option](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html) can help with that.

```
fn make_iter(do_insert: bool) -> impl Iterator<Item = i32> {
    // Explicit returns to illustrate return types matching
    match do_insert {
        true => return (0..4).chain(Some(42)).chain(4..8),
        false => return (0..4).chain(None).chain(4..8),
    }
}
println!("{:?}", make_iter(true).collect::<Vec<_>>());
println!("{:?}", make_iter(false).collect::<Vec<_>>());
```

Initialize a result to [ None](https://edp.fortanix.com/enum.Option.html#variant.None) before a loop:

```
enum Kingdom { Plant(u32, &'static str), Animal(u32, &'static str) }
// A list of data to search through.
let all_the_big_things = [
    Kingdom::Plant(250, "redwood"),
    Kingdom::Plant(230, "noble fir"),
    Kingdom::Plant(229, "sugar pine"),
    Kingdom::Animal(25, "blue whale"),
    Kingdom::Animal(19, "fin whale"),
    Kingdom::Animal(15, "north pacific right whale"),
];
// We're going to search for the name of the biggest animal,
// but to start with we've just got `None`.
let mut name_of_biggest_animal = None;
let mut size_of_biggest_animal = 0;
for big_thing in &all_the_big_things {
    match *big_thing {
        Kingdom::Animal(size, name) if size > size_of_biggest_animal => {
            // Now we've found the name of some big animal
            size_of_biggest_animal = size;
            name_of_biggest_animal = Some(name);
        }
        Kingdom::Animal(..) | Kingdom::Plant(..) => ()
    }
}
match name_of_biggest_animal {
    Some(name) => println!("the biggest animal is {}", name),
    None => println!("there are no animals :("),
}
```
